planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Gulftide' tolerates Southern heat and humidity better than many other false holly selections.

directions: Gulftide is a moderately sized, oval-habited selection of holly olive prized for its glossy, spiny, dark green leaves and its ability to handle heat and humidity better than the species, making it a long-time favorite hedge and screening plant in Southern landscapes. Small, sweetly fragrant white flowers appear tucked among the foliage in mid-fall, easy to smell before they're seen. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, and prune after flowering to maintain a dense hedge or informal screen; established plants tolerate both drought and light shade well.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to filtered sun; this is an exceptionally slow grower, so start with the largest size you can afford.

directions: Rotundifolius is an oddity among false hollies, bearing small, thick, nearly circular leaves without the spiny margins typical of the species, giving the plant a texture closer to boxwood than holly. It is a dense but extremely slow grower, taking many years to reach even modest size, which makes it well suited to small courtyard gardens, containers, or tight foundation spaces where a full-sized Osmanthus heterophyllus would be too large. Site it in partial shade to filtered sun in well-drained, humus-rich soil, and expect only light, infrequent pruning to be needed given its naturally compact habit.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; 'Radicans' resists the winter bronzing and tip blight that trouble many other Japanese cedar selections.

directions: Selected in Japan in the early 1940s originally for forestry use, 'Radicans' is a fast-growing, single-trunked Japanese cedar valued for dense, feathery blue-green foliage that holds its color through winter with far less bronzing than the species and greater resistance to tip blight and leaf spot. Its columnar-to-pyramidal form and vigorous growth rate make it a popular large-scale privacy screen and windbreak tree across the South. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and water regularly during establishment; once rooted in it tolerates heat well and needs little maintenance beyond removing the occasional dead interior branch.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; foliage color shifts from soft blue-green in summer to a rich bronze-purple in cold weather, most pronounced on exposed sites.

directions: Plume Cedar keeps the soft, feathery juvenile foliage of young Japanese cedar seedlings permanently rather than maturing into the scale-like adult needles typical of the species, giving it an unusually plush, textural look that shifts from blue-green in summer to a warm brownish-purple through winter. It grows slowly and stays bushy and rounded when young before developing a broadly pyramidal form with age, making it a good specimen or accent conifer where its winter color can be appreciated up close. Site it in full sun in rich, acidic, well-drained soil, allowing it to dry slightly between waterings once established, and avoid heavy pruning since it is naturally full-figured and slow to recover from hard cuts.
